strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: Extends RVOS to explicitly model object interactions, which are underexplored in existing datasets and methods
Substantial dataset: InterRVOS-8K with 127K expressions across 8,738 videos is the largest RVOS dataset to date; well-designed 4-stage automatic annotation pipeline
Comprehensive experiments: Thorough ablations (Table 6), zero-shot evaluation across three benchmarks (Table A2), new actor-target-aware evaluation protocol, both quantitative and qualitative results
Strong empirical results: ReVIOSa-1B outperforms larger Sa2VA-4B model (57.9 vs 55.3); consistent improvements across evaluation settings
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations and transparent dataset statistics; detailed annotation prompts in appendix
weaknesses: Critical: Dataset quality unvalidated - entire 127K dataset is automatically generated with no human evaluation, inter-annotator agreement metrics, or verification of interaction detection accuracy. No discussion of GPT hallucination risks or role assignment correctness despite claiming 'high-quality' annotations

Limited architectural novelty: ReVIOSa is a straightforward application of existing components (SAM2 + InternVL) with two appended special tokens. Interaction modeling reduces to emitting tokens; lacks sophisticated relational reasoning, structured representations, or role-aware attention

Concerning performance pattern: Interaction expressions (65.7, Table 4) significantly underperform appearance+motion (61.0) and appearance-only (59.7), suggesting either poor annotation quality or genuine model struggle with interactions—this is problematic for an 'interaction-aware' task

Narrow evaluation scope: All evaluation on own dataset; no cross-dataset validation on interaction-rich subsets of existing benchmarks; comparisons limited to Sa2VA, Referformer, LMPM; missing recent MLLM baselines

Dataset bias from filtering: Evaluation set uses filtered data to 'increase proportion of interaction-centric expressions,' making it non-representative of training distribution and potentially inflating interaction metrics

Incomplete role analysis: No performance breakdown by interaction type (unidirectional vs. bidirectional), no actor-target confusion pattern analysis, no per-role metrics—unclear how well the model distinguishes roles
Limited interaction diversity: 79.7% of interactions involve 2 objects (Figure A3), mostly simple spatial/contact interactions; no systematic interaction taxonomy or classification
Annotation pipeline robustness unexamined: Accuracy of Stage 3 interaction detection not reported; multi-stage cascading errors not analyzed; potential error propagation across 4 stages not discussed

Incomplete technical specification: Loss function weighting not fully specified (cross-entropy + Dice balance unclear); batch size 2 lacks justification; design choice rationale missing (why tokens vs. structured representations?)

Absence of failure analysis: No systematic investigation of failure modes, role-confusion patterns, problematic interaction types, or sensitivity to design choices; motion-only expressions show particularly poor performance (44.6) without explanation

strengths: Addresses a legitimate gap in RVOS by identifying the lack of interaction-aware expressions in existing datasets
Thoughtfully designed four-stage automatic annotation pipeline that systematically constructs expressions from object properties to interactions
Large-scale dataset with 127K expressions and explicit actor-target annotations, substantially denser than prior RVOS datasets
Comprehensive experimental analysis including ablation studies, zero-shot evaluation, and caption-type performance breakdown
Clear motivation with illustrative examples showing how interaction-aware expressions require distinct segmentation of participating entities
weaknesses: Critical concern: Entire dataset is automatically annotated without human validation, inter-annotator agreement metrics, or quality assessment, undermining credibility as a benchmark contribution
Minimal architectural novelty—adding two special tokens to existing models (SAM2 + LLaVA) is incremental; no learned mechanism for genuine interaction reasoning beyond prompt-based segmentation
Weak empirical evidence for interaction understanding: performance on interaction expressions (65.7 J&F) significantly lags multi-instance (70.0) and margins over baseline are marginal (60.6→65.7)
Biased evaluation methodology: actor-target-aware evaluation simply applies standard metrics to interaction samples; test set uses filtered expressions favoring interaction-centric data
Inconsistent zero-shot results undermine claims of general improvement: ReVIOSa sometimes underperforms baselines (e.g., Ref-DAVIS: 63.7 vs. 62.8)
No visualization of learned representations or attention mechanisms proving the model reasons about actor-target distinctions beyond token generation
Reproducibility concerns: no mention of dataset release, heavy dependence on specific GPT-4o/LLaMA versions, no human validation protocol described
Limited justification for task importance: no compelling case studies demonstrating when interaction-aware segmentation is critical in practice versus standard RVOS
Dataset diversity limited by modest video count (8,738 videos) relative to expression count, with analysis showing 79.7% of interactions involve only 2 objects
Missing comparisons with other recent MLLM-based RVOS methods beyond Sa2VA baseline

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task formulation addressing genuine gap in RVOS—extending beyond isolated object segmentation to model actor-target interactions is intuitive and important for real-world video understanding

Large-scale dataset contribution—InterRVOS-8K (127K expressions) is the largest RVOS dataset to date, with first explicit actor-target interaction annotations (17.7K samples) and diverse expression types
Thoughtful 4-stage automatic annotation pipeline leveraging GPT-4o and LLaMA for scalable, systematic generation of complementary interaction-aware expressions

Comprehensive experimental validation including dataset effectiveness analysis (Table 3: outperforms larger Ref-SAV), performance by caption type (Table 4), zero-shot generalization (Table A2), and ablation studies (Table 6)
Clear and well-organized presentation with effective visualizations and extensive supporting appendices providing implementation details, examples, and statistics
Demonstrates data efficiency—models trained on smaller InterRVOS subsets outperform those trained on 2.5× larger Ref-SAV dataset, validating quality of automatic annotations
Introduces actor-target-aware evaluation protocol enabling targeted assessment of interaction understanding, distinguishing this work from prior RVOS evaluations
weaknesses: Automatic annotation quality not empirically validated—critical concern for 127K-sample dataset automatically generated by GPT-4o and LLaMA without inter-annotator agreement metrics, validation sampling, or quality assessment despite acknowledged limitations

Limited architectural novelty—ReVIOSa is straightforward integration of special tokens into existing MLLM+SAM2 pipeline; joint actor-target segmentation approach, while effective, lacks technical innovation relative to recent MLLM-based RVOS methods

Core task performance modest—interaction expression performance (Table 4b: 65.7) significantly lags other categories and shows only modest improvement over appearance-only (61.0), raising questions about actual interaction understanding gains

Single-domain dataset limiting generalization—all data sourced from VidOR; no cross-domain evaluation or evidence of generalization beyond standard RVOS benchmarks which may share similar characteristics

Limited interaction complexity—79.7% of interactions involve exactly 2 objects, only 20.3% involve 3+; dataset emphasizes simple pairwise interactions rather than complex multi-object scenarios claimed in motivation

Arbitrary dataset construction choices without justification—video clip extraction strategy (first/last 1000-frame bins, first 500 frames), evaluation set filtering to increase interaction proportions, both lack ablation or sensitivity analysis

Missing critical technical comparisons—no comparison with relation detection, scene graph, or structured relationship modeling methods; baseline diversity limited to MLLM variants; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Reproducibility and availability concerns—dataset release status unclear, missing project page URL, no discussion of annotation pipeline costs/feasibility, no error analysis of multi-stage pipeline outputs

strengths: Well-motivated problem that identifies a genuine limitation in standard RVOS: the inability to distinguish semantic roles (actor vs. target) in interaction-based expressions
Large-scale InterRVOS-127K dataset (127K expressions) with systematic 4-stage automatic annotation pipeline that is thoroughly documented and reproducible
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies, layer-head selection analysis, zero-shot transfer, and dataset efficiency comparisons that support the proposed approach
Strong zero-shot transfer performance on standard RVOS benchmarks (Table A3) demonstrates that interaction-centric supervision provides robust visual-language grounding beyond the new task
Thorough technical analysis including layer-wise/head-wise attention investigation, attention mask loss justification, and visualization of how AML improves focus on object regions
Qualitative results clearly demonstrate improvements over strong Sa2VA baseline in distinguishing actor and target roles for complex interaction scenarios
weaknesses: Automatic annotation quality is a significant concern: 96% of training data (122,188 expressions) relies on GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B outputs with no explicit quality evaluation metrics, error analysis, or spot-check validation beyond the manually-refined evaluation set

Substantial unexplained performance gap: InterRVOS-Target (67.1-68.3) is 6-7 points lower than InterRVOS-Actor (73.2-75.8), raising questions about task validity and practical utility, yet this gap receives minimal discussion or error analysis

Limited technical novelty: core contributions are straightforward (two special tokens + attention mask loss) with heavy reliance on existing components (InternVL-2.5 MLLM + SAM2). AML improvement is modest (+1.5 in ablation), and no comparison with simpler alternatives is provided

Evaluation protocol lacks clarity for bidirectional interactions: dataset contains significant proportion of symmetric interactions, but how actor-target distinction applies to these cases is not explicitly explained
Limited interaction complexity scope: 80% of interactions involve 2 objects, 20% involve 3. Scalability beyond binary/ternary interactions is not demonstrated or discussed

No downstream task evaluation: paper does not validate whether separate actor-target segmentation actually improves performance on relevant applications (action recognition, interaction understanding), limiting evidence of practical impact

Dataset bias and generalization concerns: dataset is built exclusively from VidOR using automatic generation; potential for distribution bias and systematic errors from LLM outputs is not investigated

Attention Mask Loss design not fully justified: using BCE on patch-level resized masks to supervise continuous attention is a crude approximation; no comparison with alternative loss functions or regularization approaches

strengths: Clear problem motivation: identifying that standard RVOS ignores target objects in interaction expressions is valid and well-articulated
Substantial dataset contribution: InterRVOS-127K with 127K expressions and detailed 4-stage automatic annotation pipeline
Appropriate evaluation protocol: InterRVOS-Actor and InterRVOS-Target separate metrics align well with task formulation
Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating complementary contributions of special tokens (+2.6 J&F) and AML (+1.5 J&F)
Detailed layer-head selection analysis for AML (Figures 6-7) showing principled design choices based on attention patterns
Competitive performance on both proposed dataset (74.5 J&F) and standard RVOS benchmarks despite smaller model size (4B vs 7B/13B competitors)
Extensive documentation and reproducibility guidance in appendix with detailed prompts and implementation details
weaknesses: CRITICAL: No validation that actor/target distinction is actually useful—no user study or independent evidence demonstrating the task's practical value
CRITICAL: Dataset quality unvalidated—127K automatic annotations lack inter-annotator agreement metrics, error rate analysis, or quality benchmarking against gold standard
CRITICAL: Dataset validation incomplete—unclear what percentage of evaluation set required human correction, what error types exist, and whether training set has equivalent quality
CRITICAL: Main results only on authors' own dataset; core task utility claims not independently tested or validated
Limited technical novelty: architecture is LLaVA + SAM2 (existing models) with only two special tokens and one auxiliary loss—incremental contribution
Unresolved dataset-architecture improvement attribution: Table A2 suggests InterRVOS-71K succeeds partly due to dataset quality rather than architectural merit, conflating contributions

AML design appears ad-hoc: layer-head selection strategy (highest vision attention + top-4 heads) is data-dependent; improvement is modest (+1.5 J&F); causality between attention alignment and segmentation quality is unclear
SAM2 mask tracking errors may propagate through dataset—no analysis of tracking quality or error propagation impact
Arbitrary actor/target assignments: bidirectional interactions (e.g., 'people dancing') have no principled role distinction; 20.3% of interactions involve 3+ objects with unclear role assignment
Small evaluation set (5,048 test expressions) limits statistical power; no confidence intervals or significance testing provided
No failure case analysis—only successful qualitative results shown (Figures A9-A11); no analysis of which interaction types are hardest
Incomplete dataset stage validation: no quantitative evaluation of intermediate pipeline stages; reliability of GPT-4o interaction detection and temporal consistency ensurance unknown
Pseudo-caption generation with reversed actor/target roles (Stage 3) could introduce noise—not evaluated or validated
Limited generalization analysis: no evaluation on unseen interaction types, domain shift scenarios, or complex multi-object interactions (the 20.3% with 3+ objects)
Reproducibility concerns: dataset creation requires costly GPT-4o API access; no code release mentioned; computational costs not analyzed
Missing key ablations: no comparison with simpler alternatives (e.g., dual [SEG] tokens); no sensitivity analysis for AML hyperparameters; no comparison with alternative attention supervision methods
Baseline adaptation unfair: Sa2VA baseline modified by removing interaction tokens rather than better-adapted comparison; adaptation gap unclear
Dense presentation: critical details scattered between main paper and extensive appendix; some figures hard to read (attention maps)

strengths: Well-motivated task formulation extending RVOS to explicitly model actor-target interactions, addressing a genuine limitation of existing methods
Large-scale, high-quality dataset (127K expressions) with systematic 4-stage automatic annotation pipeline; valuable community resource with careful evaluation set curation
Thorough attention mask loss (AML) analysis with empirical motivation (Fig. A1), systematic layer-head selection strategy, and consistent improvements
Strong experimental results: SOTA on InterRVOS-127K, superior data efficiency compared to Ref-SAV, competitive on standard benchmarks despite smaller model size
Comprehensive experimental validation including clean ablations (Table 4), qualitative analysis, and extensive appendix supporting reproducibility
Good presentation with clear figures, organized sections, and complete reproducibility details including data annotation pipeline prompts and implementation specifications
weaknesses: Training set annotation quality not validated: 122,188 expressions rely entirely on automatic annotation without verification, error rate analysis, or inter-annotator agreement metrics; only evaluation set (5K) manually refined
Task evaluation protocol incompletely specified: unclear handling of bidirectional interactions (20.3% of dataset); role assignment ambiguity for symmetric relationships not addressed

Architectural contributions are incremental: standard MLLM→SAM2 pipeline with straightforward additions of two special tokens and auxiliary loss; limited technical novelty beyond existing Sa2VA framework

Limited failure analysis and error categorization: no systematic investigation of failure modes, no ablation on text loss component (Eq. 8), no analysis of actor-target confusion or occlusion handling

Generalization claims need qualification: performance on interaction-sparse benchmarks (MeViS, Ref-Youtube-VOS) doesn't validate core interaction-aware innovation; gains on standard RVOS primarily from AML rather than interaction modeling

Dataset coverage limitations: 35% of videos lack interaction expressions; 79.7% of interactions involve only 2 objects; limited complex multi-object scenarios; dataset built on VidOR with potential unaddressed biases
Missing experimental comparisons: no evaluation of alternative designs (sequential segmentation, single-mask approaches, explicit role prompting) making the case for proposed token design weaker

Attention mask loss has theoretical gaps: patch-level supervision justification unclear; top-4 head selection is empirically driven without sensitivity analysis; limited investigation of actor vs. target differential benefits
